extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, and law students studying U.S. interference practice
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and substantive criteria governing when and how Patent Office interference proceedings may be instituted and decided to determine priority between rival inventors (including scope, jurisdiction, requisite oaths/averments, and common examples/limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of an interference proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference is a proceeding instituted for the purpose of determining the priority of the inventive act between two or more parties who claim substantially the same patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proceeding is a contested, judicial-type proceeding within the Patent Office (the only contested case there) in which adverse parties have a right to be heard by evidence and argument; it results in a judgment awarding the patent to the lawful patentee (the one shown to be prior). See opening of §586–§587 for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is entitled to the patent (priority rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law ... awards it to that one of the claimants who first conceived the idea of the art or instrument described, provided he has used due diligence in reducing it to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain the patent in an interference the claimant must show first conception and reasonable diligence in reduction to practice. This first-to-invent/diligence standard is the substantive priority rule the interference seeks to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Patent Office jurisdiction for interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference can be instituted only between two or more pending applications, or between a pending application and an unexpired patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Office has no authority to adjudicate conflicts between patents already granted (patentees must go to the courts). Forfeited and abandoned applications have no standing in the Patent Office as the basis of any claim and are not noticed in examination of other applications. The Office’s jurisdiction extends to applications only while actually pending before it (§588).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot declare interference with expired patents or abandoned/forfeited applications
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference cannot be declared against an expired patent; forfeited and abandoned applications have no standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because an expired patent gives no enforceable right and abandoned/forfeited applications are not noticed, they cannot be parties to an interference. (Cited authorities: Ex parte Mason; Starr v. Farmer; Ex parte Spear; Ex parte Russell.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict requirement — inventions must be substantially the same
rubrics_metrics.description: An application does not conflict with another application, or an unexpired patent, unless the invention covered by each specification is substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarity of name or appearance is immaterial. The relation between two interfering inventions must be identity, equivalence, specific difference, or generic difference. Applications for identical or equivalent inventions are for the same invention. Specifically different inventions are distinct unless a genus claim is involved and not disclaimed. The examiner must look to substance (subjects/things) not merely words. (See §589 and cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of relations between inventions (identity/equivalence/specific/generic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every invention occupies toward every other the relation either of identity or of equivalence or of specific difference or of generic difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In identity/equivalence the earlier is fatal to the later; in generic difference the earlier may not bar a specific later patent but may present obstacle to the later's generic claim; in specific difference there may still be interference if one party claims the genus and the other does not disclaim. Use this classification to determine whether an interference is appropriate (§589; Banks v. Snediker explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must consider whole specification and potential claims
rubrics_metrics.description: On an interference the Claims actually made are considered, but the examiner must have regard to the whole specification and to the Claims which might be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should consider not only the literal current claims but the specification and whether lawful amendments could incorporate claims that would create conflict. Under modern rules an interference is not to be declared until the conflict appears specifically in the Claims (rules changed from earlier practice). Examples and cases (Ex parte Wheeler, Drawbaugh v. Blake) illustrate when amendments and potential claims matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal construction of interference rules to fairly limit patentees to what they can justly claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules governing interferences should be liberally construed, so that patents may be restricted to such inventions as the patentees can justly claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a guiding principle when resolving borderline conflicts: prefer constructions that fairly confine the patent to what its patentee can legitimately claim (see Drawbaugh v. Blake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance-over-form: differences in name/appearance do not avoid interference
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference may exist though the inventions have different names or different appearance; the subjects (things) matter, not the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: designs may interfere with mechanical inventions if they claim the same subject-matter; different names or appearances do not prevent interference if the inventions are equivalent; double uses can interfere; a single claim in one application may interfere with several in another. Conversely, certain claims (e.g., carrying an invention into use in a specific way) may not interfere with a claim to the invention itself (Drawbaugh v. Blake examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications conflict when anything shown in one is claimed in the other
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications conflict with each other (or with a patent) whenever anything that is shown in one is claimed in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if one application lacks an element of a combination, it can still interfere with a broader combination claim (the lesser anticipates the larger). A claim that includes matter shown in a prior patent requires notification to the patentee. (See Bell v. Gray; Marvin v. Lillie.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference requires the later applicant to claim priority of inventive act (oath requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interference cannot be instituted ... unless the later applicant claims that his own inventive act preceded that of the former applicant or patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the conflicting right is a granted patent, the later application must explicitly aver under oath that the applicant made the invention before the patentee's original application was filed (and state facts proving it). The grant of letters-patent raises a presumption of priority favoring the patentee, and applicants are rejected on reference to a prior patent unless they aver under oath their prior invention. The application-oath must show facts, not mere assertion (see Thomas v. Reese; Ex parte Nagel; Ex parte Greydon).

rubrics_metrics.name: No presumption of priority between pending original applications
rubrics_metrics.description: No presumption exists in favor of one pending original application against another; each conflicting original application is regarded as hostile to the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, a patent granted after the filing of a rival application does not have a presumption over that pending application; re-issue applications based on patents issued after rival apps likewise carry no presumption. Thus in the first four enumerated cases (two originals, original vs unexpired patent granted during pendency, etc.) no presumption requires express averments to authorize interference (§591 discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nine specific cases in which an interference may be instituted
rubrics_metrics.description: In accordance with these principles an interference can be instituted in the following cases: (1) Between two or more original conflicting applications; (2) Between an original application and an unexpired patent granted during the pendency of such original application; (3) Between an original application and an application for the re-issue of a patent granted during the pendency of such original application; (4) Between two or more applications for the re-issue of patents granted on applications pending at the same time; (5) Between an original application and an unexpired patent granted before such application had been filed, provided the applicant, after the rejection of his application upon reference to the patent, avers on oath that he made the invention before the original application of the patentee was filed; (6) Between an original application and an application for the re-issue of a patent granted before such original application was filed, provided the applicant avers on oath that he made the invention before the original application for the patent sought to be re-issued had been filed; (7) Between two or more applications for the re-issue of patents whose original applications were not pending at the same time, provided the applicant for re-issue of the later patent avers on oath that he made the invention before the original application on which the earlier patent issued had been filed; (8) Between an application for re-issue and an unexpired patent, provided the original applications for each patent were pending at the same time, and the re-issue applicant avers on oath that he made the invention before the original application of the other patentee was filed; (9) Between an application for the re-issue of a later unexpired patent and an earlier unexpired patent which was granted before the original application for the later patent had been filed, provided the re-issue applicant avers on oath that he made the invention before the filing of the original application for the earlier patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerated list clarifies where presumptions arise and when explicit oath/averments are required to overcome prior patents. The treatise explains which of these produce presumptions of priority and which do not (§591).

rubrics_metrics.name: First procedural step — notice and exact statement of conflicting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in an interference is to secure from the adverse parties an exact statement of their conflicting claims and give notice thereof to the applicants or applicant and patentee, as the case may be, and shall direct the primary examiner to proceed to determine the question of priority of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application should not automatically trigger an interference solely because it contains a claim embraced in an unexpired patent; ordinarily the application is rejected on reference to the patent. An interference is declared only when the applicant makes the required oath/averments. If the record conclusively establishes priority for one party, an interference should not be declared (to avoid frivolous proceedings). However, no prima facie showing on the record can prevent a later applicant from claiming an interference if he makes proper averments under oath (Ex parte Nagel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and anti-patterns: improper divisional applications and frivolous interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: No interference will be declared with an improper divisional application; an interference which is frivolous because the record presents conclusive proof in favor of one party should not be instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should refuse to declare interferences in cases where the record already conclusively establishes priority, or where the application is an improper divisional; interferences should be limited to those situations contemplated by the rules. The treatise cites Ex parte Holt and related cases as authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a patent issued without prior interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent issues on one of two pending applications without an interference, the patentee will have no advantage on that account over his rival, but an interference will be declared as if no patent had been granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuance of a patent does not automatically defeat a rival pending application; the Office will still treat the competing applications as hostile and may declare an interference or allow contesting rights consistent with the rules (see Gordons. Withrington; Smith v. Barter).
